subject: Critical Thinking
title: System 1 vs. System 2: The Two Minds
description: A fast breakdown of System 1 vs. System 2: The Two Minds for builders.

hook.text: You have two thinking systems. One is fast and automatic. The other is slow and lazy. Guess which wins.

buildup.text: System 1: instant, intuitive, effortless. It catches a ball, reads a face, and jumps to conclusions.

discovery.text: System 2: deliberate, logical, effortful. It does math, weighs evidence, and checks System 1's work.

twist.text: System 2 is lazy. It usually accepts System 1's snap judgments without checking. That's where biases thrive.

climax.text: Most biases are System 1 errors that System 2 didn't bother to catch.

punchline.text: Thinking slow is hard. That's why we rarely do it.

quiz.question: Why do most cognitive biases occur?
options: System 2 lazily accepts System 1's snap judgments

details.summary: Daniel Kahneman's dual-process model describes System 1 as fast, intuitive, and automatic, while System 2 is slow, deliberate, and effortful. Most cognitive biases originate from over-reliance on System 1.
details.whyItMatters: Knowing which system is driving your thinking lets you decide when to trust your intuition and when to engage deliberate analysis.
takeaways: System 1 is fast and effortless but error-prone
System 2 is accurate but slow and mentally costly
Most decisions default to System 1 without your awareness

faq.question: How can you tell whether System 1 or System 2 is driving a decision?
faq.answer: If the answer came instantly without effort, System 1 is in charge. If you had to concentrate, calculate, or deliberately weigh options, System 2 engaged. The speed and effort of your thinking is the clearest signal.

faq.question: Why does System 2 not always correct System 1 errors?
faq.answer: System 2 is lazy by design. Engaging it costs mental energy, and the brain conserves that energy by default. Unless something triggers doubt or surprise, System 2 endorses whatever System 1 produces.
